In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from geologic studies the Natural Remanent Magnetizations (N.R.M.) were analyzed with the aid of a.c. magnetic field and thermal demagnetization techniques. In the case of three folded formations the characteristic remanent magnetizations could be proved to be acquired before the subsequent folding took place. These formations are the Upper Silurian Almaden volcanics, the Upper Carboniferous-Lower Permian Bucaco Formation of Portugal and the Eocene basalts of the Lisbon region. All three other Upper Carboniferous- Lower Permian sample groups of Spain yield similar directions of magnet- ization. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. Furthermore, several samples of each group were subjected to thermal demagnetization. For this treatment cores were drilled (diameter 25 mm, height 22 mm) from the hand samples oriented in the paraffin cubes. The demagnetization was carried out stepwise, the samples being heated and cooled again to room temperature in a furnace placed in a zero ambient field. The directions and intensities of the samples, being remeasured after each step, yielded extra information besides the a.c. magnetic field demagnetization, for instance on blocking temperatures and constitution of the N.R.M. For an extensive description of the furnace, I refer to Mulder and Zijderveld (in preparation). Ordovician and Silurian Previous investigations In an earlier presentation of part of this study (Van der Voo, 1967) I described the paleomagnetism of two sample groups of volcanics from Almad6n and Atienza (Table I, no.2,3). The directions of magnetization of the well-dated Upper Silurian Almaden volcanics (10 samples, 2 sites, 2 flows) have been analyzed with the aid of a.c. magnetic field demagnetizations. One of the two components, which were present in all samplds, had a direction parallel to the present-day geomagnetic field and is likely to be secondary. The difference in attitude of the two flows permits the application of the unfolding test and proves the other component to be pre-tectonic. The Atienza andesites have been collected at six sites from at least four petrographically different units (Van der Voo, 1967). The 33 samples yielded after elimination of the small secondary component very consistent “characteristic” directions. We adopt here the term “characteristic magnetization” for this component, because conclusive proof of the primary character of the residual component revealed by progressive demagnetization is lacking (no unfolding test). the Spanish Meseta, the redbeds of Alcazar de San Juan (Table I, no.20) were the only Triassic rocks to yield a characteristic direction of magnetization. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. INTRODUCTION Mistastin Lake (63” 22’W, 5 5”52’N) occupies an elliptical northeast trending depression, approximate- ly 17 by 11 km in size, cut into the moderately rugged, barren hills of western Labrador (fig. 1). The lake is surrounded by small buttes of flat lying vol- canic rocks. A sample from a butte at the west end of the lake gave a whole rock potassium-argon age of 202 f 13 million years [l] . Metamorphosed Precam- brian rocks, cut by dikes of igneous rocks, are ex- posed on islands in the lake [2] . The structure as a whole is a crater of the type of the Clearwater Lakes [3], and Manicouagan [4]. This isolated occurrence of presumably Upper Triassic rocks offers a favourable opportunity to (1) complement our scanty paleomagnetic data for this period, (2) determine the minimum angular standard deviation of paleomagnetic vectors obtain- able over an area of about 100 km2 under optimum conditions, (3) verify th

This paper describes and analyzes paleomag- netic data obtained from the volcanic rocks of Mis- tastin Lake. 2. KILBOURNE Tucson, Arizona 85719 Paleomagnetism of Some Rocks from the Mesaverde Group, Southwestern Wyoming and Northeastern Utah ABSTRACT The results of this investigation suggest that a viscous partial thermoremanent magnetization may be important for preserving paleomagnetic direc- tions in some sedimentary rocks. INTRODUCTION A paleomagnetic study of Upper Cretaceous (Campanian) sedimentary rocks of southwest- ern Wyoming and northeastern Utah demon- strates that rocks of weak intensity can be measured and useful information extracted from the data. Four different stratigraphic sections were sampled over a vertical interval whose location is shown on Figure 1, and the stratigraphy is summarized in Figure 2. Three magnetically oriented drill cores were collected stratigraphically at each 60-m vertical interval or as close to that interval as possible. Each core was cut into three specimens of length equal to its diameter in the laboratory. An astatic magnetometer was used to measure the directions and intensity of each specimen. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS The author gratefully acknowledges the assistance of Dr. R. L. Dubois, who directed this study, and Richard D. Champney.

Subsequent samples taken in continuous stratigraphic sequence were cut to 1-inch cylinders upon return to the laboratory and were initially measured on the same air- turbine spinner magnetometer. The alternating current demagnetization ex- periments were made on 420 cycle equipment similar to that described by Patton and Fitch (1962). All samples were tumbled about three axes during the AC demagnetization process in a region in which the residual D.C. field was less than 200 gammas. section_candidates.excerpt: Triassic, 56" N, 100" E. Introduction Graham (1 955) noted the predominance of reversed directions in Permian red- beds of the western United States. A similar observation was made on the basis of a compilation of magnetic directions by Cox & Doell (1960). Following an examina- tion of Permian lavas in Australia in which only reversed magnetic directions were observed, Irving & Parry (1963) defined the Kiaman magnetic interval, and on the basis of published data from other continents, concluded that the interval extended from the beginning of Late Pennsylvanian time until approximately the close of the Palaeozoic Era. Although the information available from Europe and North America appears to support the presence of a prolonged field reversal, the division has previously been spanned only in the Australian section. In Australia the units studied represent only a small portion of the time interval involved (Irving 1966). The present study was undertaken with the express purpose of spanning the strati- graphic zone which corresponds to the Kiaman interval. We believe that the rock units represent as complete a depositional sequence as it will be possible to find within 265 L 266 a single depositional basin. A spinner magnetometer was used to measure the magnetic directions and intensities. In many cases it was necessary to spin the samples in field-free space to eliminate the effects of susceptibility anisotropy which could occasionally be detected. Only an extremely short landing was possible on the island, although the morphology was examined in some detail from the air. A single lava on the northeast coast at latitude 24" 20' West was sampled. This body is undoubtedly of Recent to Pleistocene age, and since the geomagnetic field is thought to have been entirely of normal polarity since 0.7 million years ago (Doell ef al., 1966), the lava was expected to be of normal polarity, and this is the case (Table l(g)). Sea cliffs up to 70m high occur on the western and northwestern side of the island, however, and it is conceivable that rocks older than 0.7 million years, and therefore of possible reversed polarity, occur on the island. rvey. The result is given in Table 2 and Fig. 5, which also includes results from earlier surveys of the Macaronesian insular region (Watkins ef al. 1966a, b). The result is interpreted to be a good measure of the Miocene geomagnetic pole position for this part of the Atlantic. At the 95 per cent confidence level this is significantly different from the present spin axis, but is very similar to earlier reported Miocene pole positions for Madeira and some of the Canary Islands, suggesting similarity in average ages. It may be important to realize that identical field and laboratory methods have been used in all these studies. This reinforces the conclusions made when considering the results for each island: the Miocene is likely to be a period when the spin axis was slightly removed from its present position for a substantial period of time, and no Post-Miocene differential crustal spreading has occurred in the East-Central Atlantic. D. D. Hawkes (personal communication) has kindly examined thin sections representing most of the sites sampled in this study, and classified them according to the various stages in the differentiation sequence they are inferred to represent (see Hawkes (1966a), Table 1, p. 325). The stages he distinguishes range from early differentiates (norites and noritic dolerites), middle (pigeonite dolerite) to late (ferrodolerites). Hornblende granophyres represent heteromorphs of some pigeonite dolerites and ferrodolerites. The sites are classified petrologically in these terms, in Table 1. The progressive iron enrichment evidenced in this differentiation sequence is compatible with crystallization of basalt ma

perties; their correlation with the Minor Dyke Suite seems reasonable. Radiometric age The published data on radiometric ages of the Roraima dolerites were reviewed briefly in the Introduction. McDougall et al. (1963) clearly consider the possibility, in terms of their isotopic data, that there may be two ages of dolerite in the Roraima province, some as old as 2090 my. Sampling and measurement From two to eight orientated cores, averaging four inches in length, were obtained at each site by means of a portable gasoline-powered diamond drill (Doell & Cox 1967). Conclusions Stable, consistent palaeomagnetic data have been obtained from 19 out of 31 sites in the Roraima Intrusive Suite (excluding four Group I11 sites, correlated with the Minor Dyke Suite of younger age, and the metadolerite at site 26). Fourteen of these sites fall into two groups of seven sites each, of distinctly and significantly different orientation. Representative samples from both groups are indistinguishable petrologically and in terms of bulk magnetic properties. This difference in magnetic polarity is considered to be primary, and to date from the time of emplacement and crystallization of sills of two different ages. The suite is typically tholeitic, and the variety is such as is commonly encountered as a result of differentiation in thick dolerite hills. Some fine grained dolerites are definitely from the Minor Dyke Suite (samples at Site 24 were collected from the younger dykes which cut the main Tumatumari intrusion); others may well be chilled borders from the main Roraima Suite Intrusives. D. D. Hawkes (personal communication) has kindly examined thin sections representing most of the sites sampled in this study, and classified them according to the various stages in the differentiation sequence they are inferred to represent (see Hawkes (1966a), Table 1, p. 325). The stages he distinguishes range from early differentiates (norites and noritic dolerites), middle (pigeonite dolerite) to late (ferrodolerites). Hornblende granophyres represent heteromorphs of some pigeonite dolerites and ferrodolerites. The sites are classified petrologically in these terms, in Table 1. The progressive iron enrichment evidenced in this differentiation sequence is compatible with crystallization of basalt ma

ratios found (Hawkes op. cit.), and called for by this crystallization model. Sampling and measurement From two to eight orientated cores, averaging four inches in length, were obtained at each site by means of a portable gasoline-powered diamond drill (Doell & Cox 1967). The cores were oriented in situ with the aid of an astro-compass, (La Rochelle 1961). The three oriented hand samples from Cerro Bolivar were drilled in a press and reoriented in a sand-box. The remanence measurements were made on a spinner magnetometer (Phillips & Kuckes 1967); the alternating-field demagnetization apparatus is described by McElhinny (1963). The Curie Points and saturation magnetization measurements were made on a balance constructed by Collinson (1967). The maximum error, in orientation and measurement, is estimated to be less than 5". Results The palaeomagnetic results are summarized in Tables 1 and 2. Preliminary alter- nating field (a.f.) demagnetization of samples from several sites, in small increments up to 1000 Oe, showed 300 Oe to be the optimum field for routine demagnetization. Conclusions Stable, consistent palaeomagnetic data have been obtained from 19 out of 31 sites in the Roraima Intrusive Suite (excluding four Group I11 sites, correlated with the Minor Dyke Suite of younger age, and the metadolerite at site 26). Fourteen of these sites fall into two groups of seven sites each, of distinctly and significantly different orientation. Representative samples from both groups are indistinguishable petrologically and in terms of bulk magnetic properties. This difference in magnetic polarity is considered to be primary, and to date from the time of emplacement and crystallization of sills of two different ages. It has survived a period of heating, possibly associated with the time of emplacement of the younger sills (which ever they may be), which caused substantial leakage of radiogenic argon and strontium from minerals in the rocks, to such an extent that they can no longer be distinguished by radiometric means. The suite is typically tholeitic, and the variety is such as is commonly encountered as a result of differentiation in thick dolerite hills. Some fine grained dolerites are definitely from the Minor Dyke Suite (samples at Site 24 were collected from the younger dykes which cut the main Tumatumari intrusion); others may well be chilled borders from the main Roraima Suite Intrusives. D. D. Hawkes (personal communication) has kindly examined thin sections representing most of the sites sampled in this study, and classified them according to the various stages in the differentiation sequence they are inferred to represent (see Hawkes (1966a), Table 1, p. 325). The stages he distinguishes range from early differentiates (norites and noritic dolerites), middle (pigeonite dolerite) to late (ferrodolerites). Hornblende granophyres represent heteromorphs of some pigeonite dolerites and ferrodolerites. The sites are classified petrologically in these terms, in Table 1. The progressive iron enrichment evidenced in this differentiation sequence is compatible with crystallization of basalt ma

ratios found (Hawkes op. cit.), and called for by this crystallization model. Sampling and measurement From two to eight orientated cores, averaging four inches in length, were obtained at each site by means of a portable gasoline-powered diamond drill (Doell & Cox 1967). The cores were oriented in situ with the aid of an astro-compass, (La Rochelle 1961). The three oriented hand samples from Cerro Bolivar were drilled in a press and reoriented in a sand-box. The remanence measurements were made on a spinner magnetometer (Phillips & Kuckes 1967); the alternating-field demagnetization apparatus is described by McElhinny (1963). The Curie Points and saturation magnetization measurements were made on a balance constructed by Collinson (1967). The maximum error, in orientation and measurement, is estimated to be less than 5". Results The palaeomagnetic results are summarized in Tables 1 and 2. Preliminary alter- nating field (a.f.) demagnetization of samples from several sites, in small increments up to 1000 Oe, showed 300 Oe to be the optimum field for routine demagnetization. Conclusions Stable, consistent palaeomagnetic data have been obtained from 19 out of 31 sites in the Roraima Intrusive Suite (excluding four Group I11 sites, correlated with the Minor Dyke Suite of younger age, and the metadolerite at site 26). Fourteen of these sites fall into two groups of seven sites each, of distinctly and significantly different orientation. Representative samples from both groups are indistinguishable petrologically and in terms of bulk magnetic properties. This difference in magnetic polarity is considered to be primary, and to date from the time of emplacement and crystallization of sills of two different ages. It has survived a period of heating, possibly associated with the time of emplacement of the younger sills (which ever they may be), which caused substantial leakage of radiogenic argon and strontium from minerals in the rocks, to such an extent that they can no longer be distinguished by radiometric means. cks in North America are available from the south-west United States (Runcorn 1964, DuBois 1964), Montana (in Irving 1964), Missouri (Hays & Scharon 1966), and several parts of Canada (Fahrig et al. 1965). However, palaeomagnetic directions are singularly lacking from the widespread Pre-Cambrian exposures in the Rocky Mountain region of Colorado and Wyoming. The paucity of data can be attributed principally to the types of rocks exposed; the almost entirely high-grade metamorphic and granitic rocks are not particularly suitable for palaeomagnetic study. The magnetization of metamorphic rocks is poorly understood; the magnetization of granites generally resides in large, homogeneous grains, which are magnetically unstable. INTRODUCTION Since little is known of the palcomagnetism of Antarctica, the author joined the summer party to the Sr Rondane Mountains during the second Belgian-Netherlands Antarctic Ex- pedition (1965), as organized by the Belgian- Netherlands Antarctic Committee. The Sr Rondane Mountains are situated in East Ant- arcfica, at the border of the polar plateau, and are approximately 200 km south of the 'Base Rot Baudouin,' constructed by the 1958 pdition Antarctique Belge (leader G. de Ger- lache). During January 1965 only the western part of this 250 km long and 90 km wide moun- tain range could be visited. This area lies at 72øS, 24øE. The Sr Rondane Mountains are a gneissic complex composed of an important series of gneisses and migmatites, containing marble beds, graphite-schists, and quartzites. It is a Precam- brian sedimentary sequence, isoclinally folded and strongly metamorphosed in the upper cata- zone, with varying anatexitic phenomena and with a slight retrograde metamorphism in the mesozone [Michot and Klerkx, 1966]. The Masearene Islands, R6union, Mauritius, and Rodriguez, ap- peared to resemble the Hawaiian Islands in several respects; consequently, field work on these islands was undertaken by Ian MeDoug- all in July 1963 and a large number of orientated samples were collected for palcomagnetic work. This communication is the first of a series in which the palcomagnetic results from the Mas- carene Islands will be reported. The islands are palcomagnetically of interest for two principal reasons. First, the thick se- quences of lava flows are ideal for studying the frequencies of polarity reversals of the geo- magnetic field by combining radiometric age determinations with palcomagnetic polarity measurements on the same rock units. The results of such a study on the R6union material have been reported [Chamalaun and McDoug- all, 1966], and they showed that polarity re- versals are indeed worldwide and contempo- raneous, thus leaving little doubt as to the reality of the field reversal hypothesis. JONES' Physics Department, University o/Alberta Edmonton, Alberta, Canada Sixteen samples of kimberlite have been collected from deep underground in the Premier Mine at Cullinan in the Transvaal. The stability of the natural remanent magnetization of the samples has been well tested by alternating-field demagnetization and confirmed by thermal demagnetization. The magnetization is shown to be associated with magnetite, some of which is of primary origin and some of secondary origin. The magnetite of secondary origin was formed contemporaneously with or shortly after the emplacement of the kimberlite as a result of extensive hydrothermal alteration of primary minerals. It has not been possible thus far to decide between a thermoremanent and a chemical remanent origin for the observed magnetization. Previous paleomagnetic evidence has demonstrated that the kimberlite was emplaced in Precambrian times rather than in the Cretaceous, as was previously supposed. This evidence is supported by rec

ery great. INTRODUCTION In the Republic of South Africa there is a number of diamond-bearing kimberlite pipes. Economically, the most important occurrences are in the Kimberley region of the Cape Prov- ince and in an area to the northeast of Pretoria in the Transvaal. Mining operations have shown that the pipes of the Kimberley region intrude rocks of the Karroo system (Lower Carbonifer- ous to Lower Jurassic) of South Africa [du Toit, 1954]. They also contain inclusions of material derived from Karroo formations long since eroded away. There is thus no doubt that the pipes of the Kimberley area are post-Karroo in age and Williams [1932], referring to other writers, has suggested a mid-Cretaceous age of empIacement or even later. Of the pipes in the Pretoria area only one, that of the Premier Mine, has been exploited extensively. This pipe cuts no formations that have been positively identified as postdating the Bushveld igneous complex (1950 ñ 50 m.y. [Nicolaysen et al., 1958]), but it does contain a vast xenolith of Waterberg material. INTRODUCTION In the Republic of South Africa there is a number of diamond-bearing kimberlite pipes. Economically, the most important occurrences are in the Kimberley region of the Cape Prov- ince and in an area to the northeast of Pretoria in the Transvaal. Mining operations have shown that the pipes of the Kimberley region intrude rocks of the Karroo system (Lower Carbonifer- ous to Lower Jurassic) of South Africa [du Toit, 1954]. They also contain inclusions of material derived from Karroo formations long since eroded away. There is thus no doubt that the pipes of the Kimberley area are post-Karroo in age and Williams [1932], referring to other writers, has suggested a mid-Cretaceous age of empIacement or even later. Laboratory tests indicate a stable direction of rnagnetisa­ tion with a declination of 244° and an inclination of -75° (steeply upwards), from which the paleomagnetic pole relative to Antarctica for the Jurassic is calculated on the geocentric dipole model to have been at 59°S, 139°W: this is in agreement with results from dolerite~ of similar age from two other areas in Antarctica. ave been at 59°S, 139°W: this is in agreement with results from dolerite~ of similar age from two other areas in Antarctica. Such demonstrations of uniformity are powerful evidence for the correctness of the geo­ centric dipole model for the ancient Earth's field, and for the reliability of paleo­ magnetic results. INTRODUCTION Throughout much of Victoria Land and the Ross Sea region generally, a basement complex of metasedimentary and intrusive rocks is overlain unconformably by flat-lying sediments of the Beacon Group (see, for example, Harrington, 1958). Both the basement and the cover, particularly the cover, are cut by extensive dykes and sills known as the Ferrar Dolerites. These have been considered to be of Jurassic age (Harrington, 1958). They can be correlated with some confidence through Victoria Land to the Beardmore Glacier region, and although their correlation across the Pole to the Theron Mountains region is less certain, it is nevertheless considered probable that these dolerites all belong to the same intrusive phase_ Recent potassium-argon dating of a dolerite at Lake Vashka in the Victoria Valley at 162 million years (Evernden and Richards, 1962), and elsewhere by McDougall (1963) at from 147 to 163 million years, may be taken as confirmation of t

ir correlation across the Pole to the Theron Mountains region is less certain, it is nevertheless considered probable that these dolerites all belong to the same intrusive phase_ Recent potassium-argon dating of a dolerite at Lake Vashka in the Victoria Valley at 162 million years (Evernden and Richards, 1962), and elsewhere by McDougall (1963) at from 147 to 163 million years, may be taken as confirmation of the Jurassic age of the dolerites as a whole. The dolerites have previously been the subject of paleomagnetic studies chiefly in two widely separated regions. Results of the work in the Ferrar Glacier area were reported by Turnbull (1959). Two types of iron ore are nilned on the central Mesabi Range from within the Biwabik iron formation. The first, concentrating ore, contains coarse- grained magnetite in iron formation of the magnetite-banded oxide facies. The second, direct-shipping ore, contains soft martite and goethite with minor magnetite and specularite, and quartz as the major gangue mineral. The direct-shipping or soft ore is porous and friable, and it contains numerous slump structures. The soft ore deposits are found in areas of fracture such as anticlinal crests, and almost entirely within 500 feet of the surface. The ore bottoms on Pokegama quartzite or in unoxidized iron formation. The occurrence of the ore is unrelated to the Keweenawan dikes. Paleomagnctic measurements were made on the samples using an astatic magnetometer, and demagnetization by an alternating magnetic field was applied to test for remanence stability. The primary iron formations--the Gunflint, Biwabik, and Deerwood iron forma6ons from the Gunflint, Mesabi, and Cuyuna Ranges, respectively--appear to be contemporaneous with stable, primary chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) which, as indicated by the Gunflint iron formation, yields an Animkie paleomagnetic pole position of 94øVg, 28øN. The unaltered host rocks have a stable pre-folding remanence of probable Keewatin age, whereas the ore and adjacent altered host rocks have a stable post-folding remanence of possibly Early to Middle Keweenawan age. Clements (1903) and Abbott (1907) proposed that iron-bearing groundwater solutions metasomatically replaced the primary iron-formation in structural troughs. They came from: the Republic Mine, Marquette Range; the Groveland Mine, Felch Mountain District; and along the Menominee Range. Standard paleomagnetic pro- cedures were used to study the samples. The Negaunee and Vulcan iron formations are thought to have been deposited as primary sediments of the hematite-banded and magnetite-banded oxide facies with chemical reinanent magnetization (CRM) during the Middle Animikie. The three iron formations are thought to be contemporaneous; they have been subjected to low-, intermediate-, and high-grade thermal metamorphism, and to moderate and intense dynamic metamorphism; and they are mined as concentrating iron ores at two of the localities. ng or postfolding grouping of remanence directions. However, their mean inclination is only 3.5 ø ----- 15 ø (s.d.) from the bedding plane and their declinations are randomly oriented as shown in Figure 5b which indicates a strong bias of the remanence direction to the bedding plane of the jaspilite ore. These jaspilite ore samples exhibit a moderate magnetic anisotropy as shown by the susceptibility differences measured along orthogonal axes. The measurements show that on average, the maximum susceptibility is at least 25 percent greater than the minimum susceptibility and approximately parallel to the bedding plane. section_candidates.excerpt: the largest (250 km2 ) of the islands forming the Cook Islands (Fig. 1). The island is rugged, numerous peaks rising over 500 m, but the highest point is only 650 m. The volcanic hills are surrounded by a narrow coastal strip of coral sand and other beach deposits, usually separated from the hills by an elongated swampy depression. The coastal strip, which consists in part of raised reef and beach material, supports most of the island's population and provides the greatest area of flat land. Marshall (1930) described the volcanic geology in some detail, but presented only a small locality map. He inferred an alternating sequence of basaltic and phonolitic eruptions. More recent work by Wood and Hay (1967), illustrated by a geological map, shows that the strongly dissected landforms still display the elements of the major volcanic structures-a large basaltic cone, with younger phonolitic eruptives occupying a caldera. The latest eruptions are considered to be probably as young as late Tertiary or early Pleistocene, like those of strongly dissected Oahu, Hawaiian Islands (McDougall, 1964; McDougall and Tarling, 1963). For one group of Jurassic sandstones from the Bayburt-GUmUshane region it proved to be very difficult to determine accurately the characteristic direc- tion of magnetization: the samples contained secondary magnetizations, concealing the ancient natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.). The result is therefore regarded as unreliable. Three groups, varying in age from Permian to Eocene, contained only present-day local geomagnetic field directions and these directions are considered to be secondary. As the most simple interpretation of previous data and the above mentioned results, the author suggests the hypothesis that Turkey, the Arabian Shield and Africa have acted as one drifting unit since Late Mesozoic times. GEOLOGICAL SITUATION The eastern Pontide region (Fig.2, 3, samples BAY and VTB) The Pontide chains run from west to east along the Black Sea coast from the Zonguldak-Amasra region to the Trabzon-Rize region (Fig.1). This mountain range lies immediately to the north of a great zone of dextral strike slip faults, together forming the North Anatolian faultzone, which runs from the Sea of Marmora to Lake Van and to Erzurum in eastern Turkey. Arni (1939) and Blumenthal (1964) described the Pontide chains as a mountain range with mainly Cretaceous sediments and volcanics around a few Paleozoic nuclei. of a great zone of dextral strike slip faults, together forming the North Anatolian faultzone, which runs from the Sea of Marmora to Lake Van and to Erzurum in eastern Turkey. Arni (1939) and Blumenthal (1964) described the Pontide chains as a mountain range with mainly Cretaceous sediments and volcanics around a few Paleozoic nuclei. The geology of the Giimiishane region (Fig.2) has been described recently by Zankl (1961), who paid special attention to the volcanics of Jurassic and Cretaceous age in a north-south cross-section through the eastern Pontides. Apart from various intrusive complexes, these volcanics consist of flows of basalt, trachy-andesite, dacite, spilite and rhyolite, intercalated between sediments, tuffs and agglomerates. The marine sedi- ments in this sequence (limestones, sandstones and marls) made it possible to attribute most of the volcanics to either the Jurassic or the Early Cretaceous or the Late Cretaceous-Eocene period and to establish their correct tectonical dip. The Niksav region (Fig.3) is a continuation to the west of the GUmUshane region. Fig.I. Regional map of Turkey, showing the sample areas of Fig.2, 3 and 4. Fig.2. Irving and Parry (1963) have shown, the directions of magnetization of some Carboniferous rocks from Australia are similar to those found in Australian Permian rocks. To avoid confusion they went so far as to propose that an independent magnetic chronology be set up. The basins here studied are particularly apposite to the paleomagnetic study of the Carboniferous-Permian boundary, for there are lithologies suitable for paleomag- netic work, well dated because of the economic importance of the included coals. This time interval is not particularly well known paleo- magnetically (see, however, Creer and others 1959; Everitt and Belshe, 1960; Nairn, 1960; Collinson and Nairn, 1960). Until recently it has been generally assumed that relative movements within a continental block are unimportant, and one of the major problems has been to understand the dispersion of virtual pole positions found for some periods, such as the Carboniferous. The growing aware- ness of rotation of presumed tectonic origin, even within a continental area (Black, 1964; Kotasek and Krs, 1965; Ashworth and Nairn, 1965; Watkins, 1964; Irving and Opdyke, 1965; Kawai and others, 1962; van Hilten, 1962), necessitates the study of relatively re- stricted areas between which there are differ- ences in tectonic develop

ky Brod (Rossitz-Bohmische Brod). The nearly flat-lying sediments arc practically un- disturbed except by faulting, more marked in the Plzeii basin than in the Kladno basin. This reflects renewed activity along older tectonic lines until as late as the Tertiary. Sedimenta- tion occurred with only minor breaks (sec Table 1) until the end of the Stcphanian, with a maximum in Westphalian D and Stephanian B. The presence of Permian rocks has some- times been assumed (for example, Dorn, 1966), but has not been proven (see Havlena, 1966). The sedimentary rocks are predominantly continental sandstones and shales with eco- nomically important coal scams and some kaolin deposits. Volcanic rocks, porphyries, mclaphyres and tufls are known here as well as m the Inner Sudetic basin, and these may, as there, be related to weak movements of the Asturic phase. The (lows may show kaoliniza- tion, often taken as an indication of climate. The succession forms a sequence of alternating red and gray beds. This alternation has been attributed to climatic variation, but may equally well be due to fluctuating ground-water level consequent upon minor uplifts or depres- sions of tectonic origin, or to sea-level changes which may themselves have a climatic cause. Irving and Parry (1963) have shown, the directions of magnetization of some Carboniferous rocks from Australia are similar to those found in Australian Permian rocks. To avoid confusion they went so far as to propose that an independent magnetic chronology be set up. The basins here studied are particularly apposite to the paleomagnetic study of the Carboniferous-Permian boundary, for there are lithologies suitable for paleomag- netic work, well dated because of the economic importance of the included coals. This time interval is not particularly well known paleo- magnetically (see, however, Creer and others 1959; Everitt and Belshe, 1960; Nairn, 1960; Collinson and Nairn, 1960). Until recently it has been generally assumed that relative movements within a continental block are unimportant, and one of the major problems has been to understand the dispersion of virtual pole positions found for some periods, such as the Carboniferous. The growing aware- ness of rotation of presumed tectonic origin, even within a continental area (Black, 1964; Kotasek and Krs, 1965; Ashworth and Nairn, 1965; Watkins, 1964; Irving and Opdyke, 1965; Kawai and others, 1962; van Hilten, 1962), necessitates the study of relatively re- stricted areas between which there are differ- ences in tectonic develop

ky Brod (Rossitz-Bohmische Brod). The nearly flat-lying sediments arc practically un- disturbed except by faulting, more marked in the Plzeii basin than in the Kladno basin. This reflects renewed activity along older tectonic lines until as late as the Tertiary. Sedimenta- tion occurred with only minor breaks (sec Table 1) until the end of the Stcphanian, with a maximum in Westphalian D and Stephanian B. The presence of Permian rocks has some- times been assumed (for example, Dorn, 1966), but has not been proven (see Havlena, 1966). The sedimentary rocks are predominantly continental sandstones and shales with eco- nomically important coal scams and some kaolin deposits. Volcanic rocks, porphyries, mclaphyres and tufls are known here as well as m the Inner Sudetic basin, and these may, as there, be related to weak movements of the Asturic phase. The (lows may show kaoliniza- tion, often taken as an indication of climate. The succession forms a sequence of alternating red and gray beds. This alternation has been attributed to climatic variation, but may equally well be due to fluctuating ground-water level consequent upon minor uplifts or depres- sions of tectonic origin, or to sea-level changes which may themselves have a climatic cause. Irving and Parry (1963) have shown, the directions of magnetization of some Carboniferous rocks from Australia are similar to those found in Australian Permian rocks. To avoid confusion they went so far as to propose that an independent magnetic chronology be set up. The basins here studied are particularly apposite to the paleomagnetic study of the Carboniferous-Permian boundary, for there are lithologies suitable for paleomag- netic work, well dated because of the economic importance of the included coals. This time interval is not particularly well known paleo- magnetically (see, however, Creer and others 1959; Everitt and Belshe, 1960; Nairn, 1960; Collinson and Nairn, 1960). Until recently it has been generally assumed that relative movements within a continental block are unimportant, and one of the major problems has been to understand the dispersion of virtual pole positions found for some periods, such as the Carboniferous. The growing aware- ness of rotation of presumed tectonic origin, even within a continental area (Black, 1964; Kotasek and Krs, 1965; Ashworth and Nairn, 1965; Watkins, 1964; Irving and Opdyke, 1965; Kawai and others, 1962; van Hilten, 1962), necessitates the study of relatively re- stricted areas between which there are differ- ences in tectonic develop

ky Brod (Rossitz-Bohmische Brod). The nearly flat-lying sediments arc practically un- disturbed except by faulting, more marked in the Plzeii basin than in the Kladno basin. This reflects renewed activity along older tectonic lines until as late as the Tertiary. Sedimenta- tion occurred with only minor breaks (sec Table 1) until the end of the Stcphanian, with a maximum in Westphalian D and Stephanian B. The presence of Permian rocks has some- times been assumed (for example, Dorn, 1966), but has not been proven (see Havlena, 1966). The sedimentary rocks are predominantly continental sandstones and shales with eco- nomically important coal scams and some kaolin deposits. Volcanic rocks, porphyries, mclaphyres and tufls are known here as well as m the Inner Sudetic basin, and these may, as there, be related to weak movements of the Asturic phase. The (lows may show kaoliniza- tion, often taken as an indication of climate. The succession forms a sequence of alternating red and gray beds. This alternation has been attributed to climatic variation, but may equally well be due to fluctuating ground-water level consequent upon minor uplifts or depres- sions of tectonic origin, or to sea-level changes which may themselves have a climatic cause. The numerous pub- lished virtual pole positions show a scatter so great that Irving (1964) found it convenient to treat them in two separate groups. On the other hand, Permian rocks from the same re- gion provided virtual pole positions whose dis- persion was surprisingly small. The youngest Carboniferous results, those from the Stephan- ian of western Europe (Nairn, 1960), seemed to fall close to the Permian directions and so be distinguished from the older Carboniferous which, however, contained measurements on rocks up to Westphalian age. Everitt and Belshe (1960) attempted to attribute this dis- persion to a secondary magnetization imprinted on the original, for in most of the earlier meas- urements no magnetic stability or cleaning procedures had been carried out. Cornwell* (Received 1966 May 9) Summary The directions of magnetization and the magnetic properties of the Exeter lavas and the associated red sediments have been measured. The lavas have been placed in the Stephanian on the basis of recent age deter- minations (280 m.y.) but they are interbedded with the desert type sedi- ments typical of New Red Sandstone times in southwest England. The directions of the lavas generally show little scatter and are very resistant to both thermal and a.c. demagnetization. This is probably connected with the fact that their remanence is to a large extent due to haematite and a crystallization remanence (CRM). It is likely that the CRM was formed when the lavas were exposed to weathering soon after they were extruded in desert conditions. The palaeomagnetic pole position agrees with that established by an earlier investigation of the lavas. The associated sedi- ments are not altogether satisfactory for rock magnetic studies owing to their friable nature but yield a pole position similar to that of the lavas. 1. Introduction The direction of the Earth's main magnetic field at various localities and over the past several hundred million years has been deduced from paleomagnetic measure- ments on rocks of many types. Although a fairly complete record now exists of field direction since the Pre-Cambrian [Irving 1964, Irving (& Stott) 1960-19651, compara- tively little is known of the intensity of either the dipole or non-dipole geomagnetic fields over the period covered by the rock record. This is certainly because the experimental difficulties encountered in the determination of field intensity from rocks and the uncertainties in the interpretation of the results obtained are much greater than in the corresponding measurements of direction only. Nevertheless some field intensity results have been published, and intensity values may be derived from data presented

only. Nevertheless some field intensity results have been published, and intensity values may be derived from data presented by other authors. For the geological time scale, field intensity determinations have been presented by Momose (1963) (Upper Miocene- Upper Pliocene), Van Zijl(l961) (Triassic-Jurassic) and Briden (1966) (late Silurian- early Devonian). Approximate intensity values may also be deduced from data presented by Johnson et al. (1948) (Quaternary), Nagata (1943) (Pleistocene), Koenigsberger (1938) (Tertiary and Perm-Carboniferous) and Clegg et d. (1954) (Triassic). In addition, intensity determinations on single, or pairs of, geological specimens have been carried out by Thellier et al. (1959) (Quaternary), Weaving (1960) (Tertiary) and Wilson (1961) (Tertiary). In this paper the results of field intensity determinations from Scottish Tertiary baked contacts and dykes and Icelandic Tertiary baked laterites and lavas will be described. 2.
